opus-5.5.text:
Sure. So the basic idea is pretty simple once you see it. A language model like GPT is, at every step, producing a probability distribution over the next token, the next word or piece of a word. Then it samples from that distribution, usually with some randomness controlled by a temperature parameter. That randomness is the opening for a watermark.

Normally the randomness is truly random, or at least pseudorandom in a way nobody cares about. What I proposed, when I was working on this at OpenAI, is to replace it with a cryptographic pseudorandom function. That function takes as input the last few tokens, say the previous four or five, plus a secret key that only the company holds. It outputs numbers that look completely random to anyone who doesn't have the key. You then use those numbers to choose the next token, in a way that's carefully designed so that, averaged over the key, you're sampling from exactly the same distribution the model wanted anyway.

So, to someone without the key, the output is indistinguishable from what the model would normally produce. There's no degradation in quality, no weird word choices you could notice. That was really the key design goal. But secretly, you're systematically favoring tokens for which this pseudorandom function happens to give a high score.

Then, if someone later hands you a piece of text and asks whether it came from GPT, and you hold the key, you can go through the text, recompute the pseudorandom function on each window of tokens, and add up a score. For ordinary human-written text, that score behaves like a sum of random numbers, so it hovers around some expected value. For watermarked text, it's biased upward. With a few hundred tokens, you can typically get quite high statistical confidence, especially when the text has a reasonable amount of entropy, meaning the model actually had real choices to make. If the model is just reciting the Gettysburg Address, there's no randomness to hide a signal in, and you can't watermark it, but then it's also not very interesting text.

Now, I should be upfront about the limitations, because people sometimes oversell this. The watermark is robust to small edits. If you change a word here and there, most of the n-grams survive and the signal persists. But it's not robust against a determined attacker. You could ask the model to write in French and then translate into English with a different system. Or you could ask it to insert some word between every pair of words and then delete those. Paraphrasing with another model is another obvious attack. So I've always viewed it as something that would catch the low-effort cases, the student who just copies and pastes an essay or the bulk propaganda operation that doesn't bother covering its tracks, rather than an unbreakable solution.

There's also the policy question, which is in some ways harder than the technical one. Watermarking only helps if the companies running the models actually deploy it, and if they coordinate, because otherwise people just switch to the provider that doesn't watermark. And with open-weight models, someone can simply run the model themselves without the watermark. So the cryptography is the easy part, relatively speaking. The hard part is getting the ecosystem to adopt it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a secret-key pseudorandom function over recent tokens that determines token choices and systematically favors certain tokens.

r002.rationale: It says token selection is designed so that, averaged over the key, it samples exactly from the model’s intended distribution.

r003.rationale: It explains that a detector with the key can recompute scores over token windows in a submitted text, without needing the model’s internal probabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the basic idea is actually pretty simple once you remember how a language model like GPT generates text. At every step, it's not deterministically picking the next word. It computes a probability distribution over all the possible next tokens, and then it samples from that distribution. So there's randomness built in. If you ask it the same question twice, you'll typically get different answers.

And the key insight is that you don't actually need true randomness for that sampling step. You can replace it with pseudorandomness. So what we do is take some secret key that only OpenAI knows, and we use a cryptographic pseudorandom function, applied to the previous few tokens, to generate the random numbers that decide which token gets picked. From the user's perspective, the output looks exactly the same. The distribution over outputs is unchanged. The text is just as good, just as varied. But now there's a hidden statistical pattern baked into the choices. Among tokens that were all reasonably likely, the model will subtly prefer the ones that score well under this secret function.

Then, later, if someone wants to check whether a piece of text came from GPT, they can take the text, know the key, recompute the function over each window of tokens, and compute a score. If the text was generated by the model with the watermark, that score will be way higher than you'd expect by chance. If it was written by a human, or by some other model, it'll look like noise. And with a few hundred tokens you can get a detection that's extremely confident, basically a p-value as small as you want.

A couple of things I like about this approach. One, it doesn't degrade quality at all, because you're not forcing the model to say anything it wouldn't otherwise say, you're only controlling how it resolves its own uncertainty. Two, it's somewhat robust. If someone goes through and changes a few words, or rearranges some sentences, the signal is still there, because it's spread across every token in the text. Now, if someone takes the output and has a different language model completely paraphrase it, you'll probably lose the watermark. I'm not claiming it's unbreakable. But it raises the cost of passing off model output as your own, and for a lot of applications, like catching academic plagiarism or mass-produced propaganda, that's what you want.

r001.rationale: It says a secret key and pseudorandom function over prior tokens determine the token choices, describing a hidden deterministic selection rule.

r002.rationale: It says the output distribution is unchanged and the model subtly favors tokens among those that were already reasonably likely.

r003.rationale: It says a checker can use the text and key to recompute a score over token windows, without requiring other generation data.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is to hide a statistical signal in the choices the model makes. A language model generates text one token at a time, and at each step there are usually many plausible tokens it could choose. That gives you some room to influence the choice without noticeably changing the quality of the text.

You use a secret key to generate pseudorandom preferences among those possible tokens. Then you arrange the sampling so that the model tends to choose tokens favored by that secret rule, while still respecting the probabilities the model assigns. To a reader who doesn’t know the key, it should look like ordinary generated text.

But someone who knows the key can examine a passage and ask: how strongly do these token choices line up with our rule? Over enough text, that correlation can become extremely unlikely to have occurred by chance. That’s the watermark. It’s distributed across the passage rather than being a particular phrase or an invisible character.

The important caveat is that this is statistical evidence, not an infallible label. A very short passage might not contain enough signal, and substantial rewriting or paraphrasing can weaken or remove it. The goal is to make generated text detectably different in a way that readers wouldn’t otherwise notice.

r001.rationale: The response describes secret-key pseudorandom preferences that bias token sampling, but does not state that a deterministic rule selects the next token.

r002.rationale: It says sampling tends to favor tokens while still respecting the probabilities the model assigns.

r003.rationale: It describes checking a passage’s token choices against the secret rule to assess their correlation, so the score is based on the generated text.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to hide a statistical signal in the choices the model makes. A language model generates text one token at a time, and at each step it has a probability distribution over what token comes next. There are usually many plausible choices.

You can use a secret key to pseudorandomly favor some of those choices over others. You still want the text to look natural, so you make the bias subtle. No individual word tells you that the text was machine-generated. But over a sufficiently long passage, someone who knows the key can look for an unusually strong correlation between the token choices and that secret pattern.

Think of a coin that looks fair but is slightly biased. A few flips won't tell you much; a thousand flips might. Here, the challenge is to introduce a detectable bias without noticeably changing the quality of the writing.

The important limitation is that this isn't an indestructible stamp. Short passages may not contain enough evidence, and rewriting or paraphrasing can weaken the signal. It's a statistical way to recognize output from a system that participates in the watermarking scheme.

r001.rationale: It says a secret key pseudorandomly favors choices, but does not clearly state that a secret deterministic rule selects the next token.

r002.rationale: It describes subtly biasing plausible choices to keep text natural, but does not state that watermarked selection appears to follow the model’s predicted probability distribution.

r003.rationale: It says someone with the key can look for a correlation across a passage, but does not state that a watermark score can be calculated from the generated text alone.
